terms.name: Photorealistic
terms.what: Rendering that aims to be indistinguishable from a photograph. Accurate materials, physically correct lighting, real-world scale and proportion.
terms.effect: Looks real. The viewer shouldn't be able to tell it's CG. This requires accurate PBR materials, ray/path traced lighting, correct camera simulation (depth of field, exposure, lens distortion), and photographic imperfections (grain, chromatic aberration, slight motion blur).
pairs: Architectural visualization — clients need to see the building before it's built
Product rendering — replacing expensive photo shoots
VFX integration — CG elements must match live action
Camera simulation — depth of field, lens effects, film grain make it believable
conflicts: Stylized art — photorealism is deliberately not stylized
Low-poly, toon, or abstract work — opposite intent
Speed — photorealism requires computational time

terms.name: Clay Render
terms.what: A render with a uniform matte gray material applied to everything — no textures, no color, just form and light. Used to evaluate shape, composition, and lighting without the distraction of materials.
terms.effect: Sculptural, minimal, focused entirely on form. Every object looks like a clay maquette. Light and shadow define shape without any material complexity. Reads as clean, architectural, and study-like.
pairs: Architectural form studies — shape without materiality
3D sculpture/character modeling — evaluating form
Minimal/clean aesthetic — the reduction is the point
Soft/even lighting — soft light on clay = gentle, sculptural
Product design — shape evaluation before material application
conflicts: Material-dependent subjects — no texture or color information
Realistic rendering — clay render is an abstraction
Vivid/colorful palettes — everything is gray
terms.example: Clay render + soft directional light + architectural model + ambient occlusion → pure form study, every surface matte gray, shadows defining depth and overlap, clean and sculptural

terms.name: Cel-Shaded / Toon
terms.what: Non-photorealistic rendering that mimics hand-drawn or cartoon aesthetics. Lighting is quantized into flat color bands (lit/shadow/highlight) instead of smooth gradients. Black outlines around objects. Named after animation cels.
terms.effect: Flat, graphic, cartoon-like. Hard shadow edges instead of soft gradients. Bold outlines. Looks drawn or painted rather than rendered. The 3D geometry provides form and movement while the shading removes photorealistic complexity. Notable examples: Wind Waker, Okami, Spider-Verse.
pairs: Stylized/cartoon characters — the core use case
Bold color palettes — flat shading needs strong color choices
Graphic compositions — the flatness suits graphic design
Animation — the style was designed for moving images
Comics/manga aesthetic — outlines + flat color = comic book
conflicts: Photorealism — the opposite approach
Subtle tonal gradation — cel-shading eliminates gradients
Realistic materials — everything is flat color
terms.example: Cel-shaded + bold primary colors + black outlines + dynamic pose → comic book/anime aesthetic, flat color bands, hard shadow edges, graphic energy

terms.name: Low Poly
terms.what: 3D models built with deliberately minimal polygon counts. Originated from hardware limitations of 1990s game consoles, revived as a conscious aesthetic choice around 2013.
terms.effect: Geometric, faceted, simplified. Objects are reduced to essential forms — a tree becomes a cluster of triangles, a face becomes angular planes. The visible facets catch light differently, creating a crystalline/gem-like quality. Reads as stylized, retro, indie-game, or deliberately abstract.
pairs: Flat/pastel colors — low poly + soft color = the indie game look
Soft lighting — gentle light across faceted surfaces creates pleasant gradients
Landscape/environment scenes — low poly nature is a genre unto itself
Isometric camera — low poly + isometric = miniature world
Nostalgia/retro gaming — the early 3D callback
conflicts: Photorealism — not enough geometry for realistic surfaces
Organic/smooth forms — the facets fight smoothness
High-detail/macro — low poly has no fine detail to zoom into
terms.example: Low poly landscape + soft pastel colors + isometric camera + warm lighting → miniature geometric world, faceted trees and mountains, soft gradients across flat surfaces, cozy indie aesthetic

terms.name: Wireframe
terms.what: Only edges and vertices rendered — no surfaces, no fills, no shading. The structural skeleton of a 3D model, showing every polygon edge as a line.
terms.effect: Technical, skeletal, transparent. You see through objects to the geometry behind them. Reads as blueprint, technical, deconstructed, or digital/matrix-like. The complexity of the wireframe reveals the density of the mesh.
pairs: Technical/engineering aesthetic — wireframe is a design tool
Digital/matrix/cyberpunk themes — the geometry of virtual reality
Overlay on solid renders — wireframe + photorealistic = "making of" look
Dark backgrounds — bright wireframe lines on black
Neon/glowing lines — wireframe as light sculpture
conflicts: Material/texture emphasis — wireframe has no surfaces
Photorealism — wireframe is an abstraction
Solid/heavy visual weight — wireframe is transparent and skeletal

terms.name: Voxel
terms.what: 3D equivalent of a pixel — a cube unit that builds 3D objects the way pixels build 2D images. Think Minecraft's block-based world.
terms.effect: Blocky, cubic, chunky. Everything is built from uniform cubes. The grid is visible and defines the aesthetic. Reads as retro-digital, game-like (Minecraft), or deliberately primitive. The uniformity of the grid creates an oddly satisfying regularity.
pairs: Retro/game aesthetic — Minecraft is the reference point
Isometric camera — voxels + isometric is a common combination
Bright/saturated block colors — each voxel is a solid color
Landscapes/environments — voxel worlds are charming
Nostalgic/playful mood — the blockiness is inherently friendly
conflicts: Smooth/organic forms — voxels are cubic by definition
Photorealism — too abstract
Fine detail — the minimum unit is one cube
cues: built entirely from small uniform cubes

terms.name: Glitch Art / Databending
terms.what: Deliberately corrupting or manipulating digital data to produce visual artifacts. In 3D: distorted geometry, fragmented polygons, RGB channel splitting, pixel sorting, moshing compression artifacts.
terms.effect: Corrupted, fragmented, digital-decay. Geometry shatters or warps. Colors split into RGB channels. Compression artifacts (JPEG moshing) create painterly smearing. Reads as digital, broken, post-internet, deliberately imperfect.
pairs: Cyberpunk — digital decay in dystopian context
Vaporwave — shared digital nostalgia
Dreamcore/Weirdcore — shared uncanny quality
VHS/analog artifacts — cross-media corruption
Neon/saturated color — the artifacts amplify vivid color
conflicts: Clean/precise rendering — glitch is the opposite
Photorealism — too abstract and broken
Natural/organic — glitch is digital-native
Minimalism — glitch adds chaos
cues: corrupted pixel smears and displaced blocks

terms.name: Retro 3D / PS1 Aesthetic
terms.what: The look of early 3D graphics from the PlayStation 1 era (1994-2000). Affine texture warping (textures swim and distort), vertex jitter (geometry wobbles), low-resolution textures, limited polygon counts, no anti-aliasing.
terms.effect: Textures that warp and shimmer as the camera moves. Geometry that jitters and pops at vertices. Chunky, low-resolution textures with visible pixels. No texture filtering — everything is crunchy. Limited draw distance with fog. Reads as retro, nostalgic, lo-fi, deliberately primitive, horror (the distortion creates unease).
pairs: Horror games — the visual instability creates tension (Puppet Combo, Iron Lung)
Nostalgia for 1990s gaming — PS1, N64, Saturn era
Low poly — the natural geometric companion
Fog/limited draw distance — hiding the pop-in
VHS/analog degradation — cross-media lo-fi
Liminal space aesthetic — PS1 + empty space = uncanny
conflicts: Photorealism — the opposite
Clean/smooth rendering — PS1 is crunchy by nature
High resolution — defeats the purpose
Modern PBR materials — wrong era entirely
terms.example: PS1 aesthetic + empty school hallway + warping textures + vertex jitter + fog + low resolution → unsettling retro horror, textures swimming, geometry unstable, liminal and nostalgic

terms.name: ASCII / Text-Based Rendering
terms.what: Rendering images using text characters (letters, numbers, symbols) as "pixels." Each character's density represents a brightness value. From early computer art to modern artistic choice.
terms.effect: Images composed entirely of typed characters. At distance, the characters blend into a recognizable image. Up close, it's pure text. Monospaced font grid structure. Reads as retro-digital, hacker, matrix-like, deliberately primitive.
pairs: Hacker/matrix aesthetic — the terminal/command line
Retro computing — early computer art
Cyberpunk — digital primitives
Monochrome (green or amber on black) — the CRT terminal palette
Wireframe — shared structural/skeletal quality
conflicts: Photorealism — too abstract
Color (usually) — ASCII is typically monochrome
Smooth gradients — the character grid is always visible
Organic softness — the grid is rigid and mechanical
cues: image built from typed text characters

terms.name: Traditional / Hand-Drawn (Cel Animation)
terms.what: Frame-by-frame animation drawn by hand on transparent cels, painted, and photographed over backgrounds. The foundation of animation from the 1920s through the 1990s. Disney's golden age, Looney Tunes, and most pre-digital animation.
terms.effect: Organic, fluid, human. Every frame shows the artist's hand — slight variations in line weight, subtle inconsistencies that create life. Characters have weight and squash/stretch. Backgrounds are often painted (watercolor or gouache) in a different, more detailed style than the flat-colored characters. Reads as classic, nostalgic, and handcrafted.
pairs: Painted backgrounds — detailed watercolor or gouache environments
Flat-colored characters — bold outlines filled with solid or simple-gradient color
Squash and stretch — exaggerated deformation conveying weight and energy
Warm color palettes — the painted backgrounds tend warm
Frame-by-frame fluidity — smooth, organic motion
Classic Disney / golden age context
conflicts: 3D/CG rendering — different dimension entirely
Photorealism — cel animation is stylized
Digital precision — hand-drawn has inherent variation
Minimal/static compositions — animation implies movement
terms.example: Cel animation style + painted watercolor background + flat-colored character + warm palette + soft lighting → Disney-esque quality, character pops against detailed painted environment, organic and alive
cues: clean inked outlines with flat colors

terms.name: Anime / Manga
terms.what: Japanese animation and comic art tradition. Broad category encompassing many sub-styles, but common visual elements: large expressive eyes, simplified facial features, detailed hair, dynamic action lines, limited animation with held poses and dramatic cuts. Spans from Astro Boy (1963) to Studio Ghibli to modern seasonal anime.
terms.effect: Stylized, expressive, dramatic. Faces are simplified but eyes are large and detailed — the eyes carry the emotion. Hair is rendered with distinct color blocks and sharp highlights. Action scenes use speed lines, impact frames, and dramatic camera angles. Limited animation (fewer frames per second) is compensated by strong poses and composition. Reads as distinctly Japanese, dramatic, and emotionally expressive.
pairs: Large expressive eyes — the genre's signature
Speed lines / action lines — diagonal streaks conveying motion
Hair highlights — sharp, stylized light reflections
Dramatic lighting — strong contrast, colored rim lights
Cherry blossoms / Japanese cultural elements — contextual markers
Dynamic camera angles — extreme low, high, and Dutch angles
Cel shading — flat color with defined shadow shapes
conflicts: Western cartoon proportions — different facial structure
Photorealistic rendering — anime is stylized
Subtle/understated expression — anime is emotionally heightened
Muted/desaturated palettes — anime tends vivid (though exceptions exist in seinen)
terms.example: Anime style + dramatic lighting + wind-blown hair + speed lines + vivid color → dynamic, emotionally intense, sharp highlights on hair, large eyes catching light, cinematic action energy
cues: hair in sharp color blocks with highlights

terms.name: Stylized CG Animation
terms.what: The look of contemporary 3D animated features: characters with caricatured proportions rendered with physically based light and materials. Pixar, DreamWorks, Illumination and Sony Pictures Animation set the conventions.
terms.effect: Rounded, appealing characters with oversized heads and eyes, simplified noses and hands. Smooth skin with a soft translucent glow where light passes through ears and fingers. Materials read true — cloth folds, individual hair strands, glossy eyes with sharp catchlights — while the shapes stay exaggerated. Warm soft key light with a bright rim, gentle bounce fill, saturated but harmonized color. Backgrounds slightly softened behind the character. Reads as polished, friendly, family film.
pairs: Soft key plus rim light — the feature-animation lighting setup
Shallow depth of field — the background softened behind the character
Warm saturated palettes — harmonized, never garish
Medium close-ups — room for the expressive face
Whimsical or heartfelt subjects — the natural territory
conflicts: Gritty realism and heavy film grain — the CG finish is clean
Harsh on-camera flash — flattens the sculpted lighting
Realistic proportions — the caricature is the point
Flat 2D or cel shading — a different dimension
terms.example: Stylized CG animation + small child in a cluttered workshop + medium close-up + warm key with rim light + shallow depth of field → polished family-film charm, oversized eyes with bright catchlights, soft translucent skin, warm glow
cues: rounded caricatured shapes with oversized eyes

terms.name: Stop Motion
terms.what: Physical objects (puppets, clay, paper, found objects) photographed frame by frame with incremental movements. Laika (Coraline, Kubo), Aardman (Wallace & Gromit), Wes Anderson (Fantastic Mr. Fox, Isle of Dogs).
terms.effect: Tangible, textured, slightly uncanny. Every surface is real — you can see fingerprints in clay, fabric weave on costumes, scratches on sets. The motion is slightly jerky compared to smooth CG. The miniature scale is often visible (shallow depth of field, visible set edges). Reads as handcrafted, precious, and slightly magical.
pairs: Visible material textures — clay, fabric, wood, paper
Miniature/handcrafted sets — tiny detailed environments
Shallow depth of field — tilt-shift miniature look
Slightly jerky motion — the charm of frame-by-frame
Warm/controlled lighting — miniature sets are carefully lit
Whimsical/dark fairy tale subjects — the natural territory
conflicts: Smooth/fluid motion — stop motion is inherently choppy
Digital perfection — the medium is physical
Photorealistic scale — the miniature quality is always present
Fast/fluid action — the frame rate limits smooth movement
terms.example: Stop motion + clay character + miniature set + warm lighting + fabric textures → tangible, handcrafted, slightly uncanny, every surface real and touchable, Laika-quality craft
cues: real fabric, wood and clay textures

extras.Production specifics (Laika): Faces are **3D-printed** — modeled in Maya and ZBrush, texture-painted in Photoshop, then printed on Stratasys J750 machines (500,000+ color combinations). Faces snap on/off with coded magnets. Scale of production: Coraline had **20,000 printed faces**, ParaNorman 40,000, Boxtrolls 56,000, Kubo **64,000**. Six printers running around the clock. This is "replacement animation" — each expression is a physical object swapped between frames.

terms.name: Rotoscope
terms.what: Animation traced over live-action footage — actors perform, then artists draw over each frame. Creates a distinctive uncanny-valley quality that's simultaneously realistic and animated. A Scanner Darkly, Waking Life, Undone.
terms.effect: Hyperreal but unstable. The motion is completely naturalistic (it's traced from real actors) but the rendering is illustrated — creating a dreamlike disconnect between how things move and how they look. Lines shimmer and shift frame to frame. Reads as psychedelic, dreamlike, unsettling, or philosophical.
pairs: Dreamlike/surreal narrative — the uncanny quality suits altered states
Realistic motion — movement is naturalistic despite illustrated surface
Shifting/shimmering line quality — the frame-to-frame variation
Adult/philosophical themes — the technique is rarely used for children's content
Mixed reality — the blur between real and drawn
conflicts: Clean/consistent rendering — rotoscope shimmers and shifts
Cartoony exaggeration — the motion is too naturalistic
Stable/static imagery — the constant shifting is inherent
Traditional animation principles (squash/stretch) — rotoscope follows real physics
cues: illustrated outlines traced over realistic motion

terms.name: Pixel Art
terms.what: Digital art created at the pixel level — each pixel is deliberately placed. Resolution is intentionally low (often 16x16 to 256x256). The aesthetic of 8-bit and 16-bit era video games (NES, SNES, Game Boy). Now a deliberate art form.
terms.effect: Blocky, constrained, nostalgic. Limited resolution forces extreme simplification — every pixel matters. Limited palette (often 4-64 colors). The grid is visible and defines the aesthetic. Dithering (alternating pixel patterns) simulates gradients. Anti-aliasing is done by hand, pixel by pixel. Reads as retro gaming, indie, and deliberately constrained.
pairs: Limited color palette — 4, 8, 16, or 32 colors
Low resolution — the constraint is the point
Dithering patterns — simulating tone with pixel patterns
Game/interactive context — the native format
Isometric perspective — pixel art + isometric is a classic combination
Nostalgia for 8/16-bit era — NES, SNES, Game Boy, DOS
conflicts: High resolution/smooth curves — pixels are squares
Photorealism — too abstracted
Continuous tone — the pixel grid is always visible
Modern CG polish — the opposite aesthetic
terms.example: Pixel art + 16-color palette + isometric perspective + dithered shadows + game environment → retro 16-bit aesthetic, every pixel placed, constrained palette, charming and nostalgic

terms.name: Rubber Hose Animation (1920s-30s)
terms.what: The earliest standardized cartoon style. Named for bendy, tube-like limbs without joints. Fleischer Studios (Betty Boop, early Popeye), early Disney (Steamboat Willie), Ub Iwerks. Revived in Cuphead (2017) and Bendy and the Ink Machine.
terms.effect: Round, simple bodies with noodle limbs. Pie-cut eyes (circular with a wedge). White gloves on black hands. Everything bounces to music — even inanimate objects. High contrast black and white (though Cuphead proved it works in color). Backgrounds are surreal and dreamlike. Constant motion — nothing is still.
pairs: Vintage/retro aesthetics — the 1920s-30s era
Surrealism — the original cartoons were genuinely surreal
Art Deco — era-appropriate design language
Jazz age — the music and culture of the era
Black and white / high contrast — the original format
Film grain / projector artifacts — vintage film quality
conflicts: Photorealism — the opposite of realistic anatomy
Anime — completely different proportional system
Pixar/CG — different dimension entirely
Naturalistic movement — rubber hose defies physics joyfully
terms.example: Rubber hose style + 1930s character + pie-cut eyes + bouncing to music + black and white + film grain → Fleischer Studios energy, everything dancing, surreal backgrounds, vintage cartoon charm
cues: black and white with film scratches

terms.name: UPA / Limited Animation
terms.what: United Productions of America (1950s) revolutionized animation by rejecting Disney's realism for bold graphic design. Influence runs through Hanna-Barbera, Jay Ward (Rocky and Bullwinkle), and Cartoon Network (Dexter's Lab, Powerpuff Girls, Samurai Jack).
terms.effect: Flat color fields, geometric/angular characters, minimal detail, abstract/stylized backgrounds that are often more artistically ambitious than the characters. Limited frame count — held poses, cycling animations, economical movement. Strong graphic design: negative space, bold color, asymmetric composition. Mid-century modern design principles applied to animation.
pairs: Mid-century modern design — the shared DNA
Flat bold color — limited palette, strong contrast
Geometric character design — angular, simplified
Pop art — shared graphic boldness
Minimalist backgrounds — abstract color fields
Saul Bass / Paul Rand — shared design sensibility
conflicts: Photorealism — too abstract
Detailed anime — opposite philosophy
Ghibli's naturalism — UPA is deliberately artificial
Fluid full animation — UPA is economical by design
terms.example: UPA style + angular character + flat bold colors + abstract mid-century background + limited detail → Saul Bass energy, geometric figures, strong negative space, 1950s graphic design as animation

terms.name: Shoujo
terms.what: "Girls' anime/manga." Sailor Moon, Cardcaptor Sakura, Fruits Basket. Focus on emotion, relationships, transformation.
terms.effect: Large, extremely detailed eyes with multiple sparkle reflections. Elongated limbs, slender figures. Flowers, sparkles, bubbles as emotional overlays. Pastel colors, flowing hair, elaborate costumes. Backgrounds dissolve into abstract emotional fields (roses, starbursts). The eyes carry everything.
pairs: Lolita fashion, rococo, pastel palettes, magical girl themes, soft/warm lighting, floral motifs.
conflicts: Gritty/dark styles, military, industrial, muted palettes.

terms.name: Seinen
terms.what: "Young men's anime/manga." Berserk, Ghost in the Shell, Vinland Saga, Monster. Mature themes, complex narratives.
terms.effect: Highly detailed, realistic proportions. Heavy crosshatching and texture. Dark, moody palettes. Gritty linework. Meticulous backgrounds (architecture, landscapes). Violence with anatomical precision. Less eye stylization — closer to realistic. Atmosphere is heavy, cinematic.
pairs: Cyberpunk, gothic, dark academia, film noir, chiaroscuro, dramatic lighting.
conflicts: Cute/pastel aesthetics, shoujo sparkles, bright cheerful palettes.

terms.name: Claymation
terms.what: Stop-motion using plasticine/modeling clay. Aardman (Wallace & Gromit, Shaun the Sheep), Art Clokey (Gumby), Will Vinton (California Raisins), Laika's hybrid approach.
terms.effect: Visible thumbprint textures and surface imperfections — the signature quality. Rounded, soft forms with slightly lumpy surfaces. Micro-jitter between frames. Rich saturated colors (clay takes paint well). Bead-like eyes. Miniature but detailed sets. The "handmade" quality is the entire appeal.
pairs: Visible fingerprint/clay texture — the defining visual trait
Cottagecore — for Aardman's cozy worlds
Warm controlled lighting — miniature sets lit carefully
Whimsical subjects — the natural territory
Stop motion generally — claymation is a subset
conflicts: Anime/cel animation — different dimension
Photorealism — the lumpy handmade quality fights it
Clean digital — the whole point is tactile imperfection
Sharp/precise rendering — clay is inherently soft
terms.example: Claymation + character with visible fingerprints in clay + bead eyes + miniature kitchen set + warm lighting → Wallace & Gromit charm, handmade, every surface real, slightly lumpy perfection

terms.name: Puppetry (Felt & Foam)
terms.what: Hand and rod puppets of carved foam covered in fleece or felt, performed live from below the frame. Jim Henson's Muppets, Sesame Street, Fraggle Rock; Avenue Q on stage. Unlike stop motion it is shot in real time, so sets and lighting are full-scale TV or film.
terms.effect: Soft fabric surfaces with visible fuzz and seams where the fleece panels meet. Rounded foam heads, a wide hinged mouth that opens from the jaw, half-sphere eyes with simple dark pupils, a felt or pom-pom nose. Mitten-like hands, arms on rods hanging slightly. The puppet is cut off at the waist or sits behind a counter, window or set edge that hides the performer. Bright, even studio lighting and saturated colors. Reads as warm, comic, children's television.
pairs: High-key or three-point studio lighting — the TV-studio look
Saturated primary colors — the fabric takes bold dye
Medium shot / waist-up framing — the performer stays below frame
Full-scale practical sets — kitchens, shop counters, streets built at human scale
Fabric/felt textures — the defining surface
conflicts: Photorealistic skin — the fabric is the point
Full body / wide shots — a hand puppet has no legs to show
Miniature/tilt-shift — puppet sets are human-scale, unlike stop motion
Low-key noir lighting — fights the bright TV look, though dark comedy uses it on purpose
terms.example: Felt puppet + kitchen counter set + waist-up framing + bright studio lighting + saturated colors → children's-TV warmth, fuzzy fleece, hinged mouth mid-speech, performer hidden below the counter
cues: fuzzy fleece fabric with visible seams

terms.name: Paper / Cutout Animation
terms.what: Flat cutout pieces (paper, card, fabric) moved under camera. South Park (originally real paper, now digitally replicated), Terry Gilliam's Monty Python animations, Lotte Reiniger's silhouette films.
terms.effect: Flat 2D characters with visible "joints" where limbs connect. Limited movement — characters pivot at joints, don't deform. Layered depth from stacked planes. Paper textures visible. South Park: rigid geometric shapes, minimal animation, side-view characters. Gilliam: Victorian collage, absurdist juxtaposition, jerky movement.
pairs: Collage art — shared cut-and-assemble language
Folk art — handmade quality
DIY/punk culture — lo-fi production values
Construction paper texture — the defining surface
Zine aesthetics — shared handmade energy
conflicts: Pixar/CG — completely different dimension
Fluid animation — cutout movement is inherently stiff
Photorealism — too flat and simplified
Smooth motion — the jerkiness is inherent
terms.example: Paper cutout + construction paper texture + flat characters with jointed limbs + layered backgrounds → South Park simplicity, handmade charm, geometric shapes, deliberately limited
cues: layered flat planes with drop shadows

terms.name: Silhouette Animation
terms.what: Characters and objects as black silhouettes against lit backgrounds. Lotte Reiniger's The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926), portions of Samurai Jack, Michel Ocelot's Tales of the Night, Limbo (game).
terms.effect: Pure black shapes against colored or textured backgrounds. All detail communicated through outline and pose — no facial features, no interior detail. Forces extreme clarity of gesture and silhouette. Backgrounds often richly colored/patterned. Dramatic, theatrical, shadow-puppet quality. Intricate paper-cut detail possible in silhouette edges.
pairs: Gothic aesthetics — dark, dramatic, ornate
Fairy tale/folklore — shadow puppet tradition
Art Deco — geometric elegance in the backgrounds
High-contrast composition — black on color
Noir — shared shadow emphasis
conflicts: Facial expression — lost in silhouette
Color on characters — they're black by definition
Detailed character rendering — interior detail invisible
Shoujo anime — needs visible faces and eyes for emotion

terms.name: Ligne Claire (Clear Line)
terms.what: Belgian comic art style pioneered by Hergé (Tintin). Uniform-weight outlines, flat color fills, no hatching or crosshatching. Shadows are minimal or absent. Cartoonish characters against detailed, realistic backgrounds. Term coined by Joost Swarte in 1977.
terms.effect: Clean, readable, precise. Every element is defined by a consistent black outline filled with flat color. No tonal gradation within shapes. The simplicity is deceptive — the clarity requires extreme discipline. Reads as European comic art, precise, and deliberate.
pairs: Flat/solid color fills — no gradients within shapes
Detailed architectural backgrounds — realistic settings, simplified characters
Clean black outlines — uniform weight, no variation
Limited but vivid palette — each color is distinct and unblended
Narrative/sequential context — comics, storyboards
conflicts: Painterly texture — ligne claire is anti-texture
Atmospheric depth — the flat color prevents atmospheric perspective
Photorealistic rendering — too simplified
Heavy shadow/contrast — the style minimizes tonal variation
terms.example: Ligne claire + urban street scene + flat color + uniform outlines + detailed architecture → Tintin-esque clarity, buildings precisely rendered, characters simplified, clean and readable

terms.name: Woodcut / Linocut
terms.what: Relief printmaking — image carved into wood (or linoleum), inked, and pressed onto paper. The carved-away areas print white, the raised surface prints black (or the ink color). One of the oldest printmaking techniques (China, ~200 AD; Europe, ~1400).
terms.effect: Bold, high-contrast, graphic. Strong black-and-white opposition with minimal gray tones. Visible texture from the wood grain (woodcut) or the gouge marks (linocut). Lines are bold and slightly irregular — the medium resists fine detail. Reads as handmade, historical, folk art, or deliberately raw.
pairs: High contrast black and white — the natural output of the medium
Bold/simple compositions — fine detail is difficult to carve
Visible tool marks — gouge textures, wood grain
Limited color (if multi-block) — each color is a separate printing
Folk art / traditional context — the medium's cultural home
Strong silhouettes — the relief process favors clear shapes
conflicts: Smooth gradients — the medium produces discrete tones, not gradations
Fine detail — the carving tool limits resolution
Photorealism — too graphic and simplified
Digital cleanness — woodcut is inherently textured and handmade
terms.example: Woodcut style + bold black and white + landscape + visible wood grain texture + simple composition → dramatic contrast, handmade feel, graphic simplicity, folk art character
cues: bold black and white carved lines
visible gouge marks and grain texture

terms.name: Watercolor
terms.what: Pigment suspended in water applied to paper. Transparent — light passes through the pigment and reflects off the white paper beneath, creating luminosity. Wet-in-wet (paint on wet paper) produces soft bleeds; wet-on-dry produces hard edges. The paper texture is always visible.
terms.effect: Luminous, transparent, spontaneous. Colors glow because the white paper shines through. Edges range from soft/diffused (wet-in-wet) to crisp (wet-on-dry). Pigment pools and blooms create organic, unpredictable textures. Reads as delicate, atmospheric, and hand-crafted.
pairs: Visible paper texture — the grain shows through the paint
Soft/diffused edges — bleeding, blooming watercolor effects
Limited palette — watercolor is strongest with restrained color choices
Botanical/nature subjects — the traditional watercolor genre
Light/airy compositions — the transparency keeps things bright
Atmospheric effects — fog, mist, sky gradations
conflicts: Opaque/heavy coverage — watercolor is transparent
Dark/moody palettes — the medium trends light and luminous
Hard/graphic edges everywhere — some softness is inherent
Photorealism — the medium is too loose (hyperrealist watercolor exists but is rare)
terms.example: Watercolor + botanical illustration + visible paper texture + soft wet-in-wet backgrounds + precise wet-on-dry details → luminous flowers, soft atmospheric wash behind, paper grain visible, delicate and handmade
cues: soft pigment blooms and wet bleeding edges

extras.Landmark techniques: **Winslow Homer's ocean scenes** — wet-in-wet washes for sea and sky creating atmospheric depth, then sharp wet-on-dry strokes for wave crests and rocks. The tension between soft atmospheric washes and crisp detail strokes is his signature. **J.M.W. Turner** — watercolor pushed to abstraction, entire compositions built from translucent color washes with minimal drawing. **John Singer Sargent's watercolors** — bravura speed and confidence, each stroke placed once (no reworking), white paper preserved for highlights with surgical precision.

terms.name: Oil Painting
terms.what: Pigment in oil medium (linseed, walnut, poppy) on canvas or panel. Slow-drying, allowing extended blending and reworking. The dominant medium of Western painting from the 15th century onward.
terms.effect: Rich, deep, luminous. Colors have depth from the oil medium. Brushwork ranges from invisible glazes (Old Masters) to heavily textured impasto (Van Gogh). Reads as serious, classical, and authoritative.
pairs: Visible brushstrokes / impasto — thick paint catching light
Rich/deep color — the oil medium produces saturated, deep tones
Classical subjects — portraiture, landscape, still life
Chiaroscuro — oil painting's tonal range is unmatched
Canvas texture — the weave visible through or alongside the paint
Warm color — oil paintings tend warm due to the medium's amber quality
conflicts: Flat/graphic rendering — oil painting is dimensional and textured
Digital cleanness — the medium is inherently physical
Quick/spontaneous feeling — oil painting implies time and deliberation
Pastel/washed-out palettes — oil color is too rich (unless deliberately thinned)
terms.example: Oil painting + impasto brushstrokes + portrait + warm light + dark background → rich tonal depth, visible paint texture catching light, classical luminosity, Old Master quality

extras.Landmark techniques: **Rembrandt's layering** — dark ground, transparent glazes building luminosity, opaque highlights applied last (the light literally sits on top of the darkness). **Van Gogh's impasto** — paint applied so thickly (sometimes directly from the tube) that it casts real shadows on the canvas surface, creating a textural relief that catches light. **Vermeer's camera obscura softness** — edges so soft they appear photographic, smooth invisible brushwork, light falling with optical precision. **Sargent's bravura brushwork** — single loaded-brush strokes that simultaneously describe form, light, and material in one gesture.

terms.name: Ink Wash / Sumi-e
terms.what: East Asian painting technique using black ink (sumi) diluted to various concentrations on rice paper or silk. A single medium produces the full tonal range from deep black to pale gray. Rooted in Zen Buddhism — the brush stroke is a meditation.
terms.effect: Monochromatic (black ink only), atmospheric, minimal. The ink bleeds and diffuses on the absorbent paper, creating soft edges. A single brushstroke conveys form with maximum economy. Empty space (ma) is as important as the painted areas. Reads as contemplative, restrained, and ancient.
pairs: Monochromatic black/gray — the medium is single-color
Negative space / ma — emptiness is compositional
Minimal brushstrokes — each stroke must count
Nature subjects — bamboo, mountains, water, birds
Atmospheric perspective — distant mountains fade to pale gray
Calligraphy — text and image share the same brush
conflicts: Full color — sumi-e is monochromatic
Dense/busy compositions — the style requires breathing room
Sharp/defined edges everywhere — ink bleeds on absorbent paper
Western compositional rules — sumi-e follows different spatial logic
terms.example: Sumi-e + mountain landscape + minimal brushstrokes + vast empty space + ink gradation → mountains emerging from mist, a few decisive strokes, most of the paper empty, contemplative silence
cues: black and white ink wash painting
graded washes from pale grey to black

terms.name: Ukiyo-e (Japanese Woodblock)
terms.what: Japanese woodblock printing tradition (17th-19th century). Bold outlines, flat color areas, asymmetric composition, limited palette from multi-block printing. Subjects: landscapes, portraits, nature, theater. Key artists: Hokusai, Hiroshige, Utamaro.
terms.effect: Flat color bounded by bold black lines. No modeling or shading — color is uniform within each area. Compositions are asymmetric and often cropped unexpectedly. Strong sense of pattern and decorative surface. Colors are limited by the printing process but vivid within that constraint. Reads as distinctly Japanese, decorative, and graphic.
pairs: Bold black outlines — the defining visual element
Flat color fills — no gradation within color areas
Asymmetric/unexpected composition — Japanese compositional sensibility
Nature subjects — waves, mountains, cherry blossoms, birds
Limited but vivid palette — blues, reds, greens, earth tones
Pattern and repetition — waves, clouds, rain rendered as pattern
conflicts: Photorealistic rendering — ukiyo-e is flat and graphic
Smooth tonal gradation — the woodblock process produces flat areas
Western perspective — ukiyo-e uses its own spatial logic
Muted/desaturated color — the prints are vivid
terms.example: Ukiyo-e style + crashing wave + bold outlines + flat blue and white + asymmetric composition → Hokusai's Great Wave energy, flat color bounded by bold lines, decorative pattern, graphic power
cues: flat color inside bold black outlines

terms.name: Vector / Flat Illustration
terms.what: Digital illustration using mathematical curves (Bézier paths) rather than pixels. Clean edges at any scale. Solid color fills, minimal or no gradients. The language of modern digital illustration, iconography, and infographics.
terms.effect: Perfectly clean, scalable, geometric. No texture, no brushwork, no imperfection. Colors are flat and solid. Lines are mathematically smooth. Reads as digital, modern, corporate-friendly, and accessible. The dominant style for app illustrations, brand assets, and explainer graphics.
pairs: Flat color — no gradients, no texture
Clean geometric shapes — circles, rectangles, smooth curves
Limited/branded palettes — corporate color systems
Simple subjects — people, objects, scenes simplified to essentials
Flat design / UI context — the native environment
Scalability — works at icon size or billboard size
conflicts: Handmade/textured quality — vector is too clean
Photographic reference — too abstract and simplified
Atmospheric depth — flat color prevents depth
Emotional complexity — the simplification limits expression

terms.name: Pencil / Graphite
terms.what: Drawing with graphite pencil on paper. The most fundamental drawing medium. Tonal range from light gray to near-black through pressure and layering. Visible paper texture. Line quality ranges from precise to gestural.
terms.effect: Intimate, direct, personal. The artist's hand is always visible. Tones are built through hatching, crosshatching, blending, or layering. Paper grain shows through. The graphite has a subtle metallic sheen at heavy applications. Reads as honest, studied, and handmade.
pairs: Detailed rendering — graphite excels at fine detail
Portraiture — the tonal range captures facial dimension
Hatching/crosshatching texture — the building blocks of pencil tone
Visible paper texture — white or toned paper showing through
Sketch/study quality — the medium implies process, not finish
Monochrome — graphite is inherently gray-scale
conflicts: Vivid color — graphite is monochromatic (unless colored pencil)
Bold/graphic impact — graphite is subtle
Clean/digital precision — pencil has inherent irregularity
Flat/uniform tone — graphite builds tone gradually
cues: black and white graphite pencil drawing
fine hatched shading in grey tones

terms.name: Digital Painting
terms.what: Painting in software (Photoshop, Procreate, Clip Studio) using a stylus/tablet. Mimics traditional painting but with digital tools — layers, undo, infinite color mixing. Can imitate any traditional medium or create hybrid styles.
terms.effect: Varies hugely depending on the artist's approach. Can mimic oil painting (textured brushstrokes, rich color), watercolor (soft bleeds), or create a distinctive digital look (smooth blending, perfect gradients, no paper texture). The "concept art" look — smooth, polished, cinematic digital painting — is the most recognizable variant.
pairs: Concept art / entertainment design — the industry standard medium
Cinematic lighting — digital painting can simulate any light setup
Character design — turnarounds, expressions, poses
Environment/world building — landscapes, cityscapes, interiors
Any color palette — unlimited color mixing
conflicts: Physical medium texture — no real paper grain or paint thickness (unless simulated)
Imperfection as character — digital tools trend toward polish
Hand-crafted authenticity — the medium is inherently digital

terms.name: Risograph / Screen Print
terms.what: Layered printing with limited spot colors (1-3 inks), each applied as a separate layer. Risograph is a modern stencil duplicator; screen printing is manual. Slight misregistration between layers is characteristic. Each ink is a flat, semi-transparent color.
terms.effect: Graphic, layered, textured. Limited palette (each color is a separate ink/pass). Colors overlap to create secondary hues. Slight misalignment between layers adds organic imperfection. The ink has a distinct texture — slightly speckled, grainy, and tactile. Reads as indie, zine culture, handmade, and contemporary craft.
pairs: Limited palette (2-3 colors) — the process constrains color
Overprinting / color overlap — two inks combining into a third color
Slight misregistration — the charming imperfection of manual printing
Flat/graphic compositions — the inks print flat
Zine / indie publishing — the cultural context
Grainy/textured ink — the risograph's speckled quality
conflicts: Full color / photographic — too many colors for the process
Smooth gradients — the inks print flat
Digital precision — the charm is in the imperfection
Large editions — risograph is small-batch by nature
terms.example: Risograph + two colors (fluorescent pink + dark blue) + slight misregistration + flat graphic illustration → layered spot colors overlapping to create purple where they meet, grainy ink texture, indie zine energy

terms.name: Collage
terms.what: Composition made from cut/torn fragments of existing imagery — photographs, magazines, paper, fabric, found materials. Dada, Surrealism, and punk culture all used collage extensively. Physical or digital.
terms.effect: Layered, fragmented, juxtaposed. Different textures, scales, and source materials coexist. Visible edges where pieces are cut or torn. Scale and context shift abruptly — a giant eye next to tiny buildings. Reads as rebellious, surreal, DIY, or postmodern depending on context.
pairs: Mixed textures — photographic + drawn + typographic fragments
Surreal juxtaposition — impossible combinations from real sources
Visible cut/torn edges — the construction is part of the aesthetic
Punk/zine context — collage is the DIY art form
Layered composition — depth through stacking
Found imagery — the materials come from elsewhere
conflicts: Visual unity — collage is deliberately disunified
Clean/smooth surfaces — the edges and layers are visible
Single-medium consistency — collage mixes everything
Minimal compositions — collage tends busy
cues: clashing textures and scales layered together

terms.name: Gouache
terms.what: Opaque watercolor — pigment with gum arabic mixed with white for opacity. Unlike transparent watercolor, gouache covers the surface completely. Matte finish. Used extensively in illustration, animation backgrounds (Disney, Ghibli prep), and commercial art.
terms.effect: Matte, velvety, opaque. Colors sit on the surface rather than glowing through. Flat, even coverage with visible brushstrokes at close range. Colors dry slightly lighter. Reads as illustrative, warm, handmade, slightly retro.
pairs: Matte/flat color — the natural output
Children's book subjects — the medium's commercial home
Mid-century illustration — gouache was the industry standard
Warm, muted palette — gouache dries chalky
Nature/botanical subjects — precise but painterly
conflicts: Glossy/reflective surfaces — aggressively matte
Transparent/luminous effects — gouache is opaque
Deep saturated darks — the chalk content lightens everything
Photorealism — too painterly and flat
terms.example: Gouache + forest scene + matte flat color + warm palette + visible brushwork → velvety storybook quality, chalky but rich, handmade warmth

terms.name: Charcoal Drawing
terms.what: Drawing with burned wood (vine, compressed, or pencil charcoal) on textured paper. Extremely soft, producing deep velvety blacks. Easily smudged and blended. One of the oldest drawing materials.
terms.effect: Dark, dramatic, atmospheric. Velvety blacks graphite cannot match. Soft, smoky edges from blending. Paper texture highly visible. Tonal range from near-white (erased) to absolute black (compressed). Reads as raw, emotional, expressive, classical.
pairs: Chiaroscuro — charcoal excels at dramatic light/dark
Portraiture and figure drawing — the life drawing standard
Smudged/blended tones — the medium's signature softness
Visible paper grain — charcoal reveals surface texture
Atmospheric/moody subjects — fog, smoke, shadow
conflicts: Clean precise lines — charcoal is inherently soft
Color — pure monochrome
Fine detail — the medium is too broad
Digital precision — maximally physical
terms.example: Charcoal + portrait + chiaroscuro + smudged background + visible paper grain → deep velvety blacks, smoky blended tones, classical life-drawing intensity
cues: deep velvety blacks and smudged greys

terms.name: Pastel (Chalk & Oil)
terms.what: Two distinct media. **Chalk/soft pastels**: nearly pure pigment with minimal binder. Powdery, blendable, luminous. Degas made them famous. **Oil pastels**: pigment in oil/wax binder. Creamier, resist blending, thick visible strokes.
terms.effect: Chalk — soft, powdery, luminous. Intense saturated color from nearly pure pigment. Smooth velvety gradations. Paper color shows through (toned paper traditional). Oil — waxy, thick, textured. Bold stroke marks, colors layer rather than mix. Both read as tactile and handmade.
pairs: Toned/colored paper — the paper participates in the image
Intense saturated color — pure pigment delivers vivid hues
Impressionistic subjects — landscapes, dancers, atmospheric scenes
Soft/diffused edges (chalk) — blended pastel is inherently soft
Bold stroke marks (oil) — thick, waxy texture
conflicts: Hard clean edges — pastels blur everything
Fine detail — too soft and broad
Photorealism — too textured
Digital cleanness — the medium is maximally physical

terms.name: Etching / Engraving (Intaglio)
terms.what: Lines incised into a metal plate (copper, zinc). Etching: acid bites exposed metal through a wax ground. Engraving: burin cuts directly into metal. Plate is inked, wiped, pressed onto damp paper. Rembrandt, Dürer, Goya, Piranesi.
terms.effect: Extremely fine, precise lines on light ground. Tonal range built through hatching, crosshatching, and stipple. Slight plate tone (residual ink) creates warmth. Embossed plate mark at edges. Reads as classical, precise, intellectual, archival.
pairs: Fine crosshatching — the fundamental building block
Warm cream/sepia paper — traditional printing surface
Architectural subjects — Piranesi's etchings define the genre
Classical/historical context — maps, banknotes, scientific plates
High detail — the medium rewards meticulous work
conflicts: Bold graphic simplicity — etching is about fine detail
Color — typically single-ink monochrome
Soft/blurry edges — lines are sharp and defined
Loose/gestural marks — the medium is precise
terms.example: Etching + architectural interior + fine crosshatching + warm sepia paper → Piranesi energy, obsessive line detail, tonal depth from hatching density
cues: tone built from hatching and crosshatching

terms.name: Scratchboard
terms.what: White clay-coated board covered with black ink. Artist scratches into the surface with a sharp tool, revealing white beneath. Subtractive — drawing white on black by removing material.
terms.effect: White lines on black ground. Extremely fine, precise lines. Pure black and white — no gray tones (unless partially scraped). Distinctively sharp, thin lines. Reads as dramatic, precise, editorial. The standard for wildlife illustration.
pairs: High contrast black and white — the only two values
Fine detail / texture — fur, feathers, scales rendered hair by hair
Wildlife/nature subjects — the editorial illustration standard
Dramatic lighting — light emerging from darkness
Editorial / book illustration context
conflicts: Color — pure B&W medium
Soft/blurry effects — every mark is sharp
Light backgrounds — the ground is black
Loose/gestural work — scratchboard rewards patience
terms.example: Scratchboard + owl portrait + fine white lines on black + detailed feather texture → individual feathers scratched in, dramatic, editorial wildlife quality
cues: fine white lines scratched from black

terms.name: Stipple / Pointillism Technique
terms.what: **Stippling** (ink): tone built entirely from dots, no lines. Used in scientific and editorial illustration. **Pointillism** (paint): Seurat/Signac Neo-Impressionist technique of colored dots that optically blend.
terms.effect: Stippling — tonal gradation through dot density. No lines at all. Precise, scientific, obsessively detailed. Pointillism — vibrant color from optical mixing of individual colored dots. Shimmering, luminous surface.
pairs: Scientific/botanical subjects (stipple) — the traditional context
Luminous color (pointillism) — optical mixing produces brightness
High detail — dots render extremely fine gradations
Natural subjects — landscapes, flora, fauna
Matte paper texture — dots sit on the surface
conflicts: Clean flat color — dots create inherent texture
Bold graphic lines — the point is no lines (stipple)
Smooth blending — surface is granular at close range
Speed — both techniques are painstaking

terms.name: Cross-Hatching (as Style)
terms.what: Building tone entirely through layers of parallel lines crossing at angles. Not just a shading technique but a complete illustration approach. Foundational to pen-and-ink, engraving, and editorial cartooning.
terms.effect: Dense, textured, linear. Every tonal value constructed from visible intersecting lines. Spacing and density control darkness. Reads as editorial, literary, pen-and-ink, classical. The New Yorker illustration tradition.
pairs: Pen and ink — the natural home
Editorial / literary illustration — the book illustration tradition
Portraiture and figure work — cross-hatching models form powerfully
Limited palette (black + one accent) — the editorial tradition
conflicts: Smooth tonal gradation — lines are always visible
Painterly softness — inherently linear and crisp
Photorealism — too graphic and constructed

terms.name: Stained Glass Style
terms.what: Illustration mimicking medieval and Art Nouveau stained glass windows. Bold black outlines (lead came) enclosing areas of luminous, saturated, translucent-looking color.
terms.effect: Luminous, jewel-toned, segmented. Thick black outlines divide the composition into discrete color cells. Colors appear to glow as if backlit. Reads as sacred, decorative, medieval, or Art Nouveau.
pairs: Bold black outlines — the structural element
Jewel-tone saturated color — ruby, sapphire, emerald, amber
Backlit luminous quality — light passing through color
Religious/sacred subjects — the original context
Art Nouveau — shared organic flowing lines
Symmetrical/radial composition — rose window structure
conflicts: Photorealism — too segmented
Muted palettes — stained glass is saturated
Subtle gradation — each cell is separate
Loose/spontaneous marks — the leading is structural

terms.name: Paper Cut / Kirigami Style
terms.what: Illustration mimicking cut paper art. Flat shapes layered with shadows between planes. Cultural traditions worldwide: Chinese jianzhi, Mexican papel picado, Matisse's cutouts.
terms.effect: Flat shapes with hard edges, layered with subtle shadows between planes. No drawn lines — every form is a cut silhouette. Depth from layering, not perspective. Reads as crafted, folk art, or modern depending on execution.
pairs: Flat single-color shapes — each piece is one paper color
Layered depth with drop shadows — stacked planes
Bold/simplified forms — detail limited by cutting
Folk art / cultural motifs — global paper-cutting traditions
Limited palette — each layer is one color
conflicts: Fine line detail — no lines, only cut shapes
Tonal gradation — each piece is flat
Texture within shapes — paper is uniform
terms.example: Paper cut + layered birds and flowers + subtle shadows between layers + limited palette → Matisse cutout energy, bold silhouettes, visible depth, handmade craft
cues: flat cut-paper shapes with crisp edges

terms.name: Comic Book (American)
terms.what: Superhero-dominated American tradition. Bold black outlines, dynamic anatomy, dramatic perspective. Heavy inking with brush and nib. Key names: Jack Kirby, Jim Lee, Frank Miller, Todd McFarlane.
terms.effect: Bold, dynamic, muscular. Heavy black outlines with variable line weight. Dramatic foreshortening and exaggerated anatomy. Saturated color with strong shadows. Speed lines, impact effects. Reads as heroic, kinetic, larger-than-life.
pairs: Bold black inking — variable-weight brush lines
Dynamic/exaggerated anatomy — heroic proportions
Saturated bold color — primaries and secondaries
Dramatic foreshortening — Kirby dynamism
Action/superhero subjects — the native content
Ben-Day dots (retro) or flat digital color (modern)
conflicts: Subtle/quiet compositions — the style is loud
Soft/muted palette — too bold
Minimalism — the style is maximal
Photorealism — exaggerated by design
cues: heavy black inks with bold outlines

terms.name: Manga (as illustration)
terms.what: Japanese comic art tradition. Clean precise linework, distinctive character design (large expressive eyes), screen tone for shading. Predominantly black and white. Vast genre range. Key names: Tezuka, Toriyama, CLAMP, Junji Ito.
terms.effect: Clean, precise, expressive. Thinner, more uniform linework than American comics. Screen tone (mechanical dot patterns) for shading instead of rendered shadow. Backgrounds alternate between detailed environments and abstract emotional spaces. Characters' eyes carry enormous emotional weight.
pairs: Clean precise linework — thinner than American comic inks
Screen tone shading — mechanical dot patterns
Large expressive eyes — the emotional anchor
Black and white — the primary format
Speed lines / emotional background effects — sparkles, petals, abstract
conflicts: Painterly texture — manga is crisp and clean
Western color palettes — manga is primarily monochrome
Loose/sketchy linework — manga lines are controlled
Realistic proportions (usually) — deliberately stylized

extras.Production specifics: Professional mangakas use **B4 manuscript paper** (~257x364mm) with printed safe/trim/bleed guides; doujinshi (self-published) artists use A4. Resolution: **600 DPI** standard for B&W with screen tone. Two primary pen nibs: **G-pen** (open slit, variable line thickness with pressure — used for character outlines and bold lines) and **maru-pen** (fine, thin lines — used for eyes, hair, and detailed backgrounds). **Screen tone**: adhesive sheets of dot patterns at various densities (typically 10-60% black), cut with X-acto and burnished onto the page. Demands firm, smooth paper — thin paper creates bubbles and uneven adhesion.

terms.name: Technical / Patent Illustration
terms.what: Precise line drawings showing construction, assembly, or function of objects. Patent illustration follows strict guidelines: black on white, specific views, numbered callouts. Pure communication, no artistic expression.
terms.effect: Clean uniform-weight black lines on white. No shading except minimal hatching. Exploded views show components separated along assembly axes. Numbered callouts. Dashed lines for hidden features. Reads as engineering, institutional, objective.
pairs: Clean black lines on white — standard format
Exploded/assembly views — the signature diagram type
Numbered callouts — parts identification
Mechanical/industrial subjects — the natural content
Multiple orthographic views — front, side, top, section
conflicts: Artistic expression — technical illustration is objective
Color — typically monochrome
Atmospheric effects — information only
Organic subjects — suits manufactured objects
cues: clean uniform black lines on white

terms.name: Graffiti / Street Art
terms.what: Visual language of urban art. Graffiti: letterform-based (tags, throw-ups, wildstyle). Street art: broader (murals, stencils, wheat-paste). From 1970s NYC subway culture to global movement.
terms.effect: Bold, colorful, energetic. Exaggerated dimensional letterforms. Saturated, high-contrast color. Spray paint effects: soft overspray edges, hard stencil edges, drips and runs. Urban surface context (brick, concrete, metal). Reads as rebellious, urban, youth culture.
pairs: Spray paint texture — overspray, drips, fades
Bold saturated color — neon, primary, high contrast
Urban surfaces — brick walls, concrete, metal shutters
Dimensional letterforms — 3D block letters with shadows
Characters alongside letters — cartoon figures, faces
conflicts: Clean/polished surfaces — graffiti needs urban grit
Classical/formal composition — graffiti is anarchic
Muted/pastel palettes — too bold and saturated
terms.example: Graffiti wildstyle + dimensional letters + spray paint on brick + neon colors + drips → NYC subway energy, interlocking letters, saturated color on gritty brick
cues: spray paint with soft overspray and drips
bold saturated colors with thick outlines

terms.name: 35mm (Full Frame)
terms.what: The standard photographic film format — 24x36mm frame on 135 film. Introduced by Leica in the 1920s, it became the dominant format for the 20th century. "Full frame" digital sensors match this size.
terms.effect: The baseline. Moderate depth of field, natural perspective, visible but controlled grain. The default visual language of photojournalism, street photography, and documentary work. When people picture "a photograph," they're usually picturing 35mm characteristics.
pairs: Visible film grain — reinforces the analog, authentic quality
28-50mm focal lengths — the natural street/documentary range for this format
Slightly underexposed or pushed processing — gritty, high-contrast photojournalism look
conflicts: Ultra-clean, noise-free rendering — fights the grain/texture expectation
Medium format tonal smoothness — 35mm is grittier by nature
terms.example: 35mm film + 28mm wide angle + Kodak Tri-X 400 + available light → high-contrast black and white street photography, visible grain, deep shadows, documentary realism

extras.Associated cameras: Leica M series, Canon AE-1, Nikon FM2, Pentax K1000 (film). Canon EOS R5, Sony A7 series, Nikon Z series (digital).

terms.name: Medium Format
terms.what: Film format using 120 roll film, producing frames between 6x4.5cm and 6x17cm — two to six times larger than 35mm. The larger negative captures more detail with finer grain and smoother tonal gradations.
terms.effect: Noticeably different from 35mm. Shallower depth of field at equivalent framing (larger format requires longer focal lengths). Smoother tonal transitions. Finer grain. An overall sense of richness and dimensionality. Skin tones look more dimensional. Highlights roll off more gently.
pairs: Portrait and beauty work — the tonal smoothness flatters skin
Fashion editorial — the square 6x6 crop is a strong compositional statement
Soft directional lighting — medium format's tonal range shines with nuanced light
Shallow depth of field — the format's natural tendency, lean into it
conflicts: Gritty, lo-fi aesthetics — medium format reads as polished and intentional
Fast action/candid — the cameras are slow and deliberate by nature
Heavy grain — counteracts the format's smoothness advantage
terms.example: Hasselblad 500C + 80mm f/2.8 + Kodak Portra 160 + soft window light → rich, warm portrait with square crop, smooth skin tones, gentle highlight rolloff, fine grain, fashion editorial quality

extras.Associated cameras: Hasselblad 500C/500CM (6x6 square, NASA moon missions, fashion standard), Mamiya RZ67 (6x7, portrait workhorse), Rolleiflex (6x6 TLR, mid-century street), Fujifilm GFX series (modern digital medium format).

terms.name: Large Format
terms.what: Sheet film 4x5 inches or larger (also 5x7, 8x10). Each exposure is a single sheet loaded in a dark holder. A 4x5 frame has 15 times the area of 35mm.
terms.effect: Extraordinary resolution and detail. Virtually grainless images with smooth, continuous tonal gradation. View camera tilt/shift movements allow precise focus plane control via the Scheimpflug principle — razor-thin focus at an angle, or everything sharp front to back.
pairs: Landscape — Ansel Adams's Zone System was built for this format
Architectural photography — shift movements correct converging verticals
Fine art portraiture — the detail and tonal range are unmatched
Long exposures — the deliberate workflow encourages slow, considered work
conflicts: Spontaneity, candid, street — the camera is slow and conspicuous
Action/movement — sheet film, tripod required, no motor drive
Lo-fi or casual aesthetics — everything about large format reads as deliberate and premium
terms.example: 4x5 large format + 210mm lens + Fuji Velvia 50 + golden hour side light → hyper-detailed landscape with saturated but natural color, no visible grain, extreme depth of field via tilt, luminous quality

extras.Associated cameras: Speed Graphic, Sinar, Toyo, Linhof, Intrepid.

terms.name: Instant / Polaroid
terms.what: Self-developing film that produces a print within minutes. Polaroid SX-70, Instax, Impossible Project.
terms.effect: Soft focus, muted and slightly shifted colors, a characteristic warm cast, and the iconic white border. Colors are less saturated and lean warm. Highlights can blow out with a milky quality. Nostalgic, imperfect, one-of-a-kind feeling.
pairs: Warm, soft lighting — golden hour, window light amplify the warmth
Casual/intimate subjects — the format reads as personal and unguarded
Visible white border — strong compositional signifier, immediately recognizable
Slightly overexposed — leans into the milky highlight quality
conflicts: Technical precision — the format is inherently soft and unpredictable
High saturation — Polaroid colors are muted by nature
Dark/moody tones — the warm cast and low contrast fight heavy shadows
terms.example: Polaroid SX-70 + soft afternoon light + slightly overexposed + white border → intimate, warm, nostalgic snapshot with muted pastels and dreamy softness
cues: soft focus with muted warm colors

terms.name: Disposable Camera
terms.what: Single-use cameras with fixed-focus plastic lenses and built-in flash. Kodak FunSaver, Fujifilm QuickSnap.
terms.effect: Soft/slightly blurry focus (plastic lens), harsh direct flash with hard shadows, oversaturated colors from cheap film, vignetting at edges. Amateur snapshot quality — imperfect, casual, spontaneous.
pairs: Harsh on-camera flash — the defining look, don't soften it
Nighttime/party scenes — flash overpowering darkness is the iconic disposable shot
Oversaturated color — cheap film pushes reds and greens
Slight motion blur — the slow shutter speed + flash freeze creates ghosting
conflicts: Sharp detail — the plastic lens physically cannot resolve it
Studio-quality lighting — defeats the raw, amateur aesthetic
Muted/desaturated tones — disposable film is punchy and oversaturated
terms.example: Disposable camera + direct flash + nighttime party + motion blur → blown-out faces against dark background, hard shadows, oversaturated skin tones, 90s nostalgia energy
cues: harsh direct flash with hard shadows

terms.name: Smartphone / Computational
terms.what: Small-sensor cameras (iPhone, Pixel, etc.) with wide-angle equivalent lenses (~26mm) and heavy computational processing — HDR stacking, noise reduction, portrait mode depth simulation.
terms.effect: Ultra-sharp but flat. Computational HDR compresses dynamic range, making shadows and highlights unnaturally even. Deep depth of field from the small sensor (everything in focus). Portrait mode simulates bokeh via software but the falloff looks synthetic compared to optical blur. Colors are saturated and consistent. Recognizably "phone photo."
pairs: Social media/casual framing — selfie angles, arm's-length perspective
Harsh or mixed lighting — computational HDR handles it (that's the point)
Deep depth of field — lean into the "everything sharp" quality rather than fighting it
conflicts: Shallow depth of field — software bokeh always looks synthetic
Film grain or analog texture — the computational pipeline removes imperfection
Cinematic or editorial quality — the flat HDR look is the opposite of cinematic dynamic range
terms.example: iPhone + HDR + direct front flash + selfie angle → flat, sharp, social media snapshot with even exposure, deep focus, slight wide-angle distortion on close faces

terms.name: Daguerreotype
terms.what: The first commercially practical photographic process (1839). A silver-coated copper plate sensitized with iodine vapor, exposed in a camera, then developed over heated mercury. Each image is a unique, mirror-like object — no negative, no copies.
terms.effect: Mirror-like reflective silver surface — the image appears positive or negative depending on viewing angle. Extraordinary fine detail for the era. Monochromatic silver-gray tonal range. Visible plate edges and imperfections. Spectral, ghostly, precious quality. Exposures of 15-60+ seconds meant subjects had to hold perfectly still, creating a rigid formality.
pairs: Formal portraiture — the rigid pose requirement became a compositional feature
Dark backgrounds — common for the era, focuses attention on the subject
Historical/period subjects — the process IS the 19th century
Ornate frames and cases — daguerreotypes were presented as precious objects
Memento mori aesthetic — the ghostly quality suits mortality themes
conflicts: Motion/action — impossible with long exposures
Color — silver monochrome only
Casual framing — the process demands formality
Modern aesthetics — too antique
terms.example: Daguerreotype + formal portrait + dark background + silver-plate surface + visible plate edges → ghostly, precious, mirror-like tones, 1850s formal intensity

terms.name: Wet Plate Collodion
terms.what: Photographic process (1851-1880s) where a glass or metal plate is coated with collodion, sensitized in silver nitrate, exposed while still wet, then developed immediately — all within about 15 minutes. The photographer is also a chemist.
terms.effect: Only sensitive to blue/UV light — blue eyes render pale/ghostly, red lips go dark, freckles become prominent. Visible pour lines from the collodion coating. Dark or uneven edges with chemical artifacts (drips, streaks). Hauntingly sharp in the center with organic falloff. A raw, handmade quality that's simultaneously precise and imperfect.
pairs: Intense portraiture — the blue sensitivity creates eerie, compelling faces
Civil War-era aesthetic — the process defines that visual period
Dark/moody backgrounds — common studio practice
Environmental portraits — subject in their world
Memento mori — the ghostly rendering suits mortality themes
conflicts: Color accuracy — blue-sensitive only
Movement — multi-second exposures
Even edge-to-edge quality — chemical artifacts at edges
Polished/digital aesthetics — too raw and handmade
terms.example: Wet plate collodion + intense portrait + blue-sensitive rendering + visible pour lines at edges + chemical artifacts → haunting, sharp center with organic edge decay, Civil War-era intensity
cues: black and white wet plate collodion photograph
visible pour lines and chemical streaks

terms.name: Tintype
terms.what: Variation of wet plate collodion on thin lacquered iron (not tin). Popular 1860s-1900s for affordable street and carnival portraiture. Sturdy and cheap — the "instant photo" of the 19th century.
terms.effect: Similar to wet plate but darker, more compressed tonal range (the dark iron base absorbs highlights). Lower contrast. Visible surface texture from the metal plate. Can appear laterally reversed (direct positive). Warm brownish or cool bluish tones depending on chemistry. Rougher, more democratic quality than daguerreotype.
pairs: Americana / Old West aesthetic — the process defines frontier portraiture
Folk/rough portraiture — less precious than daguerreotype
Hand-tinted color accents — cheeks, jewelry, buttons painted by hand
Carnival/sideshow imagery — the street portrait tradition
conflicts: High contrast / bright whites — the iron base suppresses them
Precision/sharpness — rougher than daguerreotype
Modern polish — too antique and rough
cues: dark compressed tones on a metal plate

terms.name: Pinhole Camera
terms.what: The simplest possible camera — a lightproof box with a tiny hole, no lens. Light passes through the pinhole and projects an inverted image. Exposure times range from seconds to hours. Can be made from anything.
terms.effect: Infinite depth of field (everything from inches to infinity is equally in/out of focus), soft overall image quality (no true sharpness anywhere), natural vignetting, motion blur from long exposures. No lens distortion whatsoever. Dreamy, primitive, lo-fi quality.
pairs: Long exposure — inherent to the process
Architecture / landscapes — the infinite depth of field suits sweeping scenes
Experimental/art — the simplicity is the point
Solargraph — multi-month exposures tracking the sun's path across the sky
Contemplative/meditative mood — the slow process dictates the aesthetic
conflicts: Fast action / sharpness — physically impossible
Shallow depth of field — infinite focus is the only option
Handheld shooting — exposures are too long
Crisp modern photography — everything is soft
terms.example: Pinhole camera + long exposure + architectural interior + infinite depth of field + natural vignetting → soft, ethereal, everything equally in focus, dreamy lo-fi

terms.name: Infrared Photography
terms.what: Photography using film or sensors sensitive to near-infrared light (700-1200nm wavelength), invisible to the human eye. Achieved via infrared-sensitive film (Kodak Aerochrome, Ilford SFX) or a modified digital sensor with an IR-pass filter.
terms.effect: Green foliage turns bright white or magenta/pink (the "Wood effect" — chlorophyll reflects IR strongly). Skin becomes pale and waxy. Blue skies turn near-black. Veins become visible under skin. Atmospheric haze disappears. Color infrared (Aerochrome) produces surreal false-color with magentas and reds replacing greens.
pairs: Landscape — the white/magenta foliage is the signature
Surreal/dreamlike aesthetic — the color inversion is otherworldly
Summer foliage — maximum chlorophyll = maximum IR effect
High contrast black and white — IR B&W has deep blacks and bright whites
Clear skies — IR turns blue sky nearly black
conflicts: Overcast/flat light — less dramatic IR effect
Autumn/dead foliage — no chlorophyll to reflect IR
Indoor scenes — limited IR sources
Naturalistic color — IR is the opposite of natural
terms.example: Infrared + Kodak Aerochrome + forest landscape + summer + clear sky → magenta trees, deep black sky, surreal false-color, dreamlike and alien

terms.name: Ultra Wide Angle (10-20mm)
terms.what: Extremely wide field of view, approaching or exceeding 100 degrees.
terms.effect: Dramatic spatial exaggeration. Near objects appear much larger than far objects. Barrel distortion stretches edges. Straight lines near frame edges curve outward. Creates immersion and scale — rooms look bigger, landscapes more expansive, foreground subjects loom.
pairs: Architectural interiors — exaggerates space, makes rooms look grand
Low-angle shots — subject towers over viewer dramatically
Leading lines — the distortion amplifies converging perspective
Landscape with strong foreground — wildflowers in front, mountains behind, both huge
conflicts: Portraiture — extreme facial distortion at close range
Flat/compressed backgrounds — ultra-wide does the opposite
Subtle compositions — the lens imposes itself on every image
terms.example: 14mm ultra-wide + low angle + interior architecture + natural light from windows → dramatic room perspective, converging lines, exaggerated depth, light spilling across expansive space
cues: near objects huge, far objects tiny
lines curving at the frame edges

terms.name: Wide Angle (24-35mm)
terms.what: Wider than normal field of view (63-84 degrees). Workhorse for photojournalism, street photography, and environmental portraiture.
terms.effect: Expanded spatial relationships — foreground and background feel farther apart. Mild barrel distortion at edges. Deep depth of field comes easily. 28mm and 35mm are especially natural-feeling — wide enough for context, not so wide as to distort.
pairs: Street photography — captures subject and environment together
Environmental portraits — person within their world, context visible
Documentary/photojournalism — the "being there" perspective
Deep depth of field — everything sharp, situational awareness
conflicts: Tight headshot portraiture — mild but unflattering facial distortion under ~50mm
Background isolation — wide angles keep backgrounds in focus and visible
Compressed/stacked compositions — wide does the opposite of telephoto compression
terms.example: 35mm + f/8 + street scene + hard midday sun → deep focus, everything sharp foreground to background, expanded spatial relationships, documentary immediacy
cues: near objects large, far objects small
stretched distortion at the frame edges

terms.name: Short Telephoto / Portrait (70-105mm)
terms.what: The classic portrait range. Mild perspective compression that flatters facial features.
terms.effect: Gentle compression — nose doesn't protrude, face looks proportional, background pushed farther away. At wide apertures (f/1.2-f/2.0), produces creamy background blur that isolates the subject. The 85mm f/1.4 is the iconic portrait lens — sharp eyes, smooth skin tones, melted background.
pairs: Rembrandt or butterfly lighting — compression + directional shadow = classic editorial portrait
Wide aperture (f/1.2-f/2.0) — maximizes the signature subject separation
Medium format — both push toward rich tonality and shallow depth
Beauty/fashion — flattering perspective, subject isolation, skin detail
conflicts: Environmental context — the tight framing and shallow depth erase surroundings
Deep depth of field (f/11+) — defeats the lens's core strength
Ultra-wide establishing shots — opposite intent
terms.example: 85mm f/1.4 + Rembrandt lighting + Kodak Portra 400 + wide open → warm, intimate portrait, one eye tack sharp, background dissolved into creamy warm bokeh, dimensional skin tones

terms.name: Telephoto (200-400mm)
terms.what: Strong compression, very narrow field of view. The world appears stacked and flattened.
terms.effect: Extreme perspective compression — distant objects appear almost the same size as near objects. Backgrounds look like flat walls. Heat haze and atmospheric effects become visible. Depth of field is extremely shallow even at moderate apertures.
pairs: Wildlife — close framing from safe distance
Surveillance/voyeuristic aesthetic — the distance between photographer and subject is felt
Stacked urban scenes — buildings, cars, people compressed into layers
Atmospheric haze — long focal lengths pick up air density
conflicts: Wide establishing shots — the opposite intent
Interiors — physically impossible
Spatial depth/dimension — telephoto flattens everything
terms.example: 300mm + f/4 + heat haze + crowded street → flattened perspective, people stacked in layers, shimmering atmospheric distortion, voyeuristic distance

terms.name: Fisheye
terms.what: Ultra-wide lens (8-16mm) with extreme barrel distortion — straight lines curve dramatically. Field of view up to 180 degrees. Circular fisheye produces a round image; full-frame fisheye fills the rectangle with distortion.
terms.effect: Spherical distortion of the entire frame. Center bulges toward viewer. Straight lines become curves. Surreal, immersive, or playful quality.
pairs: Skateboarding/action sports — the iconic Thrasher magazine aesthetic
Low-angle shots — looking up at subject with curved architecture wrapping around
Psychedelic/surreal imagery — the distortion is the point
Tight spaces — captures everything in a small room
conflicts: Natural proportions or straight lines
Portraiture — extreme facial distortion
Architectural accuracy — curves everything
terms.example: Fisheye + low angle + skatepark + harsh daylight → curved concrete forms, skater looming overhead, extreme spatial distortion, action sports energy

terms.name: Macro
terms.what: Lens designed for extreme close-up photography, reproducing subjects at 1:1 ratio or greater. Common focal lengths: 60mm, 90mm, 100mm, 120mm.
terms.effect: Reveals detail invisible to the naked eye. Depth of field is razor-thin — at 1:1 and f/2.8, only a few millimeters in focus. The rest dissolves into blur. The world looks alien at this scale.
pairs: Product detail shots — texture, material, craftsmanship visible
Beauty/skin texture — pores, freckles, individual lashes
Nature (insects, flowers) — the classic macro subject
Abstract compositions — everyday objects become unrecognizable up close
Ring flash or diffused light — even illumination on tiny subjects
conflicts: Context/environment — you can't see anything beyond the tiny focus area
Deep depth of field — physically impossible at macro distances without extreme f-stops
Movement — the thin focus plane means any shake loses the shot
terms.example: 100mm macro + f/4 + ring flash + water droplets on leaf → extreme detail, droplets sharp against soft green bokeh, light refracting through water, each vein of the leaf visible

terms.name: Tilt-Shift
terms.what: Specialty lens that tilts the lens plane relative to the sensor (controlling focus plane angle) and shifts parallel to the sensor (controlling perspective).
terms.effect: Two distinct uses: 1. **Tilt for selective focus**: Creates a wedge-shaped focus plane — the "miniature/diorama" effect where only a thin band is sharp. Real-world scenes look like toy models. 2. **Shift for perspective control**: Corrects converging vertical lines when pointing up at buildings.
pairs: Aerial/overhead city views — the miniature effect is strongest from above
Architectural photography — shift corrects perspective distortion
Saturated color — amplifies the toy-like quality of tilt miniatures
Bright, even lighting — midday sun on a tilt-shift cityscape maximizes the model look
conflicts: Natural depth of field — tilt-shift focus is intentionally artificial
Low light/moody scenes — the miniature effect needs clear visibility to read
terms.example: Tilt-shift + overhead cityscape + midday sun + saturated color → city looks like a detailed architectural model, thin band of focus across buildings, everything above and below softly blurred
cues: real scene looking like a toy model

terms.name: Anamorphic
terms.what: Cinema lens with oval-shaped glass elements that squeeze a wide field of view onto a standard sensor, then "de-squeeze" in post or projection. Standard squeeze ratios: 1.33x and 2x. The defining lens of widescreen cinema — Blade Runner, any J.J. Abrams film, most blockbusters.
